messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 48

He is seventy-one now, a quiet man from Oceania who has spent most of his life making sense of the world through color. Before the attack, his days move with the steady rhythm of a painter’s life. He works alone, often from first light, stretching canvas, mixing oils, studying how shadows settle across a wall or the edge of a cup. He never marries, and over the years he grows used to his own company. He has friends, a few regulars who stop by his studio, and he likes the predictability of small routines: coffee from the same stall, the same route through the market, the same bench where he sometimes sits and sketches strangers.

The day of the bombing begins like any other. He is in a crowded public square, carrying a paper bag with brushes and a new palette knife. He remembers noticing a child chasing pigeons and thinking the morning light has an unusual clarity. Then there is a sound he cannot fit into anything familiar—sharp, enormous, close enough to seem inside his body. The ground jumps. Glass bursts outward. For a few seconds, everything becomes white dust, screaming, and the metallic taste of blood. He is knocked down hard onto one shoulder. When he lifts his head, he sees bodies scattered in ways the human body should not be. A woman nearby is crying for someone who does not answer. He smells smoke and something burned that he later realizes is flesh. He crawls behind an overturned table and stays there, half deaf, convinced another explosion is coming.

In the weeks afterward, people tell him he is lucky. He has cuts, bruising, a fractured collarbone, but he survives. He says little. At first he believes the worst part is over because he is home again, sleeping in his own bed. But sleep changes almost immediately. He wakes gasping, hearing the blast before he is fully conscious, his heart pounding so hard he has to sit on the edge of the mattress and press his hand to his chest. Sometimes the dream is exact—the child, the pigeons, the woman calling out. Sometimes it is only sound and dust and the certainty that he is about to die.

He stops going to the market. He takes the long way around busy streets so he does not have to pass the square. If a truck backfires, he freezes where he stands. Once, months after the attack, a stack of metal trays crashes in a café and he drops to the floor before he understands where he is. He notices the shame on other people’s faces before he can get back into his chair. After that, he avoids cafés too.

Painting, which has always been where he feels most himself, begins to change. For a while he cannot work at all. He stands in front of a blank canvas and feels anger rising in him, hot and irrational, because the emptiness reminds him of the white dust after the explosion. When he does paint, the images narrow. He tells himself he is experimenting, but over time his canvases fill with broken lines, scorched tones, faceless figures, windows shattered into impossible geometry. He becomes frustrated by red paint. Sometimes just opening a tube of cadmium red makes him think of blood drying on pavement, and he has to leave the room.

His world grows smaller without him fully intending it to. He keeps the radio low so sudden news bulletins will not startle him. He checks exits wherever he goes and prefers to sit facing doors. In crowds he feels his body tighten, his eyes scanning bags, hands, expressions. He hates this vigilance but cannot turn it off. He tells himself he is being sensible. Still, he knows the difference between caution and the exhausting alertness that follows him everywhere.

There are moments he cannot explain to others. In the late afternoon, when sunlight hits floating dust in the studio, he is back in the square, throat full of grit. The smell of fireworks at a holiday celebration makes him abruptly nauseated. On anniversaries of the attack, he becomes withdrawn and irritable without first realizing why. Friends say he seems distant. He knows they are right. He lets calls go unanswered. It is easier not to explain why a simple outing can leave him trembling for hours afterward.

He also carries a quieter burden: the fact that he survived while others did not. He thinks of the woman he heard crying out, of the child he noticed just before the blast, and he wonders what right he has to grow old in his studio, complaining about sleep and noise and memory. Sometimes he studies his own hands—paint-stained, still steady enough to work—and feels both gratitude and accusation.

In the present, he still paints most days, though more slowly than before. He keeps the studio door locked. He startles at sirens. He sleeps in fragments. He says the world no longer feels ordinary; it feels conditional, as if safety is a surface that can split open without warning. And yet he continues to return to the canvas, trying to make an image that is true to what happened without having to stand in that square again.
